name: Faraday's Law of Induction
statement: A changing magnetic field through a loop induces a voltage in it.
statementAccent: changing magnetic field through a loop induces a voltage
meaning: It is not a magnetic field but its change over time that drives an electromotive force around a circuit, and a current if the circuit is closed. The faster the magnetic flux through the loop changes, the larger the induced voltage.
mechanism: The induced electromotive force equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop. The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change that produced it, a consequence of energy conservation. Flux can change two ways (the field itself varying in time, or the circuit moving through a spatially varying field) giving transformer and motional electromotive force.

examples.text: Rotating a coil in a magnetic field continuously changes the flux through it, producing the electromotive force that generates almost all of the world's electricity.
A changing current in one coil produces changing flux that induces a voltage in a second coil: essentially Faraday's original iron-ring experiment, and the reason grids can step voltages up and down.
An alternating field induces eddy currents directly in ferromagnetic cookware, heating the pan without heating the surface beneath it.

variants.name: The Maxwell–Faraday equation
variants.text: The differential field form, one of Maxwell's four equations, describing the fields directly and independently of any physical circuit: the exact, exception-free version of the law.

variants.name: Lenz's law
variants.text: The rule that fixes the direction of the induced current, supplying the minus sign in Faraday's law and expressing the underlying conservation of energy.

whyItMatters: It is the principle behind electric generators, transformers, and much of modern technology: the discovery that magnetism and motion can be turned into electricity. Its subtle circuit exceptions, and the field equation that resolves them, also helped motivate special relativity.

working.lead: Change the flux to get a voltage
working.text: induce an electromotive force by varying the field, moving the circuit, or changing the loop's area or orientation: anything that changes the flux.
the induced current always opposes the change that made it, so read off its direction from what it resists.

working.lead: Fall back to the field equation for edge cases
working.text: for tricky moving-circuit problems, combine the Lorentz force with the exact Maxwell–Faraday equation rather than the naive flux rule.

limits: The naive 'flux rule' has genuine exceptions when the circuit's boundary is chosen carelessly or moves oddly: the homopolar generator produces an electromotive force even though the computed flux does not change with time. The always-correct procedure combines the Lorentz force law with the Maxwell–Faraday equation, which is itself exact within classical electromagnetism. So the law is an extremely well-verified engineering rule with known edge cases, underpinned by an exact field equation.
misreadings: It is a changing field, not a steady one, that induces a voltage: a strong but constant magnetic field through a loop induces nothing. And the simple flux rule is not exception-free; certain moving-circuit cases need the underlying field equation and the Lorentz force to get right.
origin: Discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831, whose iron-ring experiment showed a changing current in one coil inducing a current in another. Joseph Henry made the discovery independently around the same time but published later; strict priority is contested, though Faraday published first and holds the primary credit.
